summary.text: For \(k\ge 60\), set \(n=2k+1\); any nonzero matrix entry gives primes \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\) summing to \(2n=4k+2\), so absence of such a decomposition would make the entire matrix zero and contradict its assumed nonzero determinant. The remaining cases \(1\le k\le 59\) are settled by explicit prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
M_n=(m_{ij})_{0\le i,j<n}
\]
be the \(n\times n\) integer matrix defining \(A228623(n)\). Thus
\[
m_{ij}=\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Here the expressions are evaluated as natural numbers. For \(0\le i,j<n\), the subtractions do not truncate: indeed \(j<n\le n+i\) and \(i<n\le n+j\). Consequently these natural-number expressions agree with the corresponding ordinary integer differences. By definition,
\[
A228623(n)=\det M_n.
\]

Assume the stated nonvanishing conjecture:
\[
\text{for every odd }n>120,\qquad A228623(n)\ne0.
\]
We prove that, for every positive integer \(k\), the number \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

First dispose of the finite range \(1\le k\le59\). The following table gives, for every such \(k\), two primes \(p,q\) whose sum is \(4k+2\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
k&(p,q)&p+q&k&(p,q)&p+q\\ \hline
1&(3,3)&6&2&(3,7)&10\\
3&(3,11)&14&4&(5,13)&18\\
5&(3,19)&22&6&(3,23)&26\\
7&(7,23)&30&8&(3,31)&34\\
9&(7,31)&38&10&(5,37)&42\\
11&(3,43)&46&12&(3,47)&50\\
13&(7,47)&54&14&(5,53)&58\\
15&(3,59)&62&16&(5,61)&66\\
17&(3,67)&70&18&(3,71)&74\\
19&(5,73)&78&20&(3,79)&82\\
21&(3,83)&86&22&(7,83)&90\\
23&(5,89)&94&24&(19,79)&98\\
25&(5,97)&102&26&(3,103)&106\\
27&(3,107)&110&28&(5,109)&114\\
29&(5,113)&118&30&(13,109)&122\\
31&(13,113)&126&32&(3,127)&130\\
33&(3,131)&134&34&(7,131)&138\\
35&(3,139)&142&36&(7,139)&146\\
37&(11,139)&150&38&(3,151)&154\\
39&(7,151)&158&40&(5,157)&162\\
41&(3,163)&166&42&(3,167)&170\\
43&(7,167)&174&44&(5,173)&178\\
45&(3,179)&182&46&(5,181)&186\\
47&(11,179)&190&48&(3,191)&194\\
49&(5,193)&198&50&(3,199)&202\\
51&(7,199)&206&52&(11,199)&210\\
53&(3,211)&214&54&(7,211)&218\\
55&(11,211)&222&56&(3,223)&226\\
57&(3,227)&230&58&(5,229)&234\\
59&(5,233)&238&&&
\end{array}
\]
Every equality in the last column of each block is immediate arithmetic and has the form \(p+q=4k+2\). The primality assertions are also a finite elementary check. More explicitly, aside from the primes \(3,5,7,11,13\), every number appearing in the table lies between \(19\) and \(233\). Since \(\sqrt{233}<16\), a composite number in that range would have a prime divisor among \(2,3,5,7,11,13\). Direct division of the displayed numbers by those possible divisors shows that none is divisible by any of them. Thus all displayed summands are prime. This proves the desired conclusion for \(1\le k\le59\).

It remains to consider \(k\ge60\). Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd, and
\[
n=2k+1\ge121>120.
\]
The assumed conjecture therefore gives
\[
\det M_n=A228623(n)\ne0. \tag{1}
\]
We show that this forces a representation of \(4k+2\) as a sum of two primes.

Suppose, to the contrary, that no such representation exists; that is, suppose there are no primes \(p,q\) satisfying
\[
4k+2=p+q. \tag{2}
\]
Consider an arbitrary entry \(m_{ij}\) of \(M_n\), where \(0\le i,j<n\). If this entry were \(1\), then by the definition of the matrix the two natural numbers
\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i
\]
would both be prime. As observed above, because \(i,j<n\), both subtractions are exact. We may therefore add these expressions as ordinary integer differences and obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
p+q
  &=(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)\\
  &=2n\\
  &=2(2k+1)\\
  &=4k+2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(p,q\) would be primes satisfying (2), contrary to our supposition. Hence no entry of \(M_n\) can be \(1\). Since every entry is, by definition, either \(0\) or \(1\), every entry must be \(0\). Therefore \(M_n\) is the zero matrix.

Because \(n=2k+1>0\), this matrix has at least one row and column. The determinant of a nonempty zero square matrix is zero. Indeed, in the Leibniz expansion of its determinant, each term is a product containing matrix entries, and every such product contains a zero factor. Consequently
\[
\det M_n=0,
\]
contradicting (1).

The supposition that no prime representation exists is therefore false. Hence for every \(k\ge60\) there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
4k+2=p+q.
\]
Together with the explicit table for \(1\le k\le59\), this proves that every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is a sum of two primes.
